entries.old: Cards are accepted at resorts, hotels, malls and larger restaurants, and US dollars are widely taken in tourist zones. Carry pesos in cash for local restaurants, small shops, guaguas (local buses) and rural areas, and prefer ATMs inside banks or resorts.
entries.new: No official source we could read describes how widely cards are accepted in the Dominican Republic. Australia's Smartraveller warns that credit card and ATM fraud are common and advises using ATMs in daylight hours at hotels, shopping centres or other controlled areas.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: December to April brings dry, sunny weather and the least humidity — peak beach season. Hurricane season officially runs June–November, with the highest storm risk August–October.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the hurricane season runs from early June to the end of November.
entries.note: Replaced with the climate statement the cited source supports.

entries.old: Duty-free allowance per adult: 20 packs of cigarettes (or 25 cigars or 200 g of tobacco), up to 5 liters of alcoholic drinks, and gifts up to USD 500 (once every 3 months). | Fresh fruit, plants and animal products are restricted. Declare them on the e-Ticket or leave them at home.
entries.new: (none)
entries.note: Only what an official source states is kept, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: All-inclusive resorts are only one side of the country — Santo Domingo's Zona Colonial (the oldest European city in the Americas), Samaná's whales (January–March) and Cabarete's kitesurfing are easy add-ons; use pesos and expect a different price level outside resorts.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports it.

entries.old: Motoconchos (moto-taxis) are cheap but the most dangerous way to get around — helmets are rare and traffic is chaotic. Road accidents are a leading cause of tourist injury; prefer registered taxis or ride-hailing apps.
entries.new: The UK government says motorbike taxis (motoconchos) are often driven badly and do not always provide passengers with a helmet. Prefer registered taxis.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Hurricane season peaks August–October. Travel is usually fine, but buy insurance that covers weather disruption and follow local guidance if a storm approaches.
entries.new: The UK government says the Caribbean hurricane season normally runs from June to November. Buy insurance that covers weather disruption and follow local guidance if a storm approaches.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Ecuador uses the US dollar, so there is nothing to change. Cards work in Quito, Cuenca, Guayaquil and Galápagos hotels, but cash rules in markets, buses and small towns, and almost nobody can break a USD 50 or 100 note, so bring small bills.
entries.new: The UK government says US dollars and the 5, 10, 25 and 50 centavo coins minted in Ecuador are the only legal currencies, and that credit cards are generally accepted in cities but not elsewhere. Australia's Smartraveller advises carrying US$1 notes, because many smaller shops and taxi drivers don't change large notes.
entries.note: Rewritten to the UK and Australian advice.

entries.old: June to September is the dry season in the highlands, best for Quito, Cotopaxi and the Quilotoa loop. The Galápagos works all year — cooler, choppier seas from June to November and warmer, calmer water from December to May.
entries.new: The UK government says the rainy season usually runs from October to May and can last until June; Canada gives December to May, and Australia's Smartraveller gives December to May on the coast and May to November in the Amazon east of the Andes. No official source names a best season.
entries.note: The highland-dry-season and Galápagos sea-condition claims had no official source.

entries.old: United States dollar (Ecuador has been dollarised since 2000)
entries.new: US dollar
entries.note: ISO 4217 lists the US dollar for Ecuador.

entries.old: Strict biosecurity applies to the Galápagos: no fresh food, seeds, plants or animal products may be carried to the islands, and bags are screened before departure from the mainland. | Exporting pre-Columbian artefacts or protected wildlife products — including some shell and coral souvenirs — is prohibited. | Drone use requires authorization in national parks and is heavily restricted in the Galápagos.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: None of the three notes (Galápagos biosecurity rules, the ban on exporting pre-Columbian artefacts, drone authorisation) could be confirmed on an official page.

entries.old: The Galápagos has its own charges on top of your flight: the USD 20 transit control card on the mainland and the national park entrance fee, which was raised to USD 200 for most foreign adults in August 2024. Both are payable in cash. Budget for them separately.
entries.new: The Galápagos has its own charges on top of your flight: Canada's travel advice says you must buy the Galápagos Transit Control Card at the Galápagos Governing Council counter in Quito or Guayaquil airport, and the islands' protected areas charge a separate entrance fee. Budget for both.
entries.note: The USD 20 and USD 200 amounts and the cash-only claim could not be confirmed on an official page.

entries.old: Quito sits at about 2,850 m and Cotopaxi far higher. Take the first day slowly, and remember the equatorial sun burns fast at altitude even when the air feels cool.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller says many areas of Ecuador are higher than 2,500 m, including Quito at 2,800 m, and altitude sickness is a risk. Ascend slowly and make sure your insurance covers evacuation from altitude.
entries.note: The equatorial-sun claim had no source.

entries.old: Security in the coastal provinces and along the Colombian border has been volatile since 2023, with states of emergency and curfews imposed at short notice. Travel between cities by day, use registered taxis or apps, and check local news before changing plans.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller says the government may declare a state of emergency at any time and curfews may be imposed. The UK government reports a 60-day state of emergency in eight provinces, declared on 15 September 2026, with a greater police and military presence. Check current advice and follow local authorities.
entries.note: Attributed to the UK and Australian advice; the travel-by-day and taxi advice was dropped.

entries.old: No separate visa — the Galápagos is part of Ecuador — but there are extra steps. Register at the Galápagos Governing Council desk in Quito or Guayaquil airport and buy the USD 20 transit control card before check-in, have your bag screened for food and plant material, and pay the national park entrance fee on arrival, which is USD 200 for most foreign adults. You also need a return ticket, confirmed accommodation or a tour booking, and valid health insurance.
entries.new: No separate visa — the Galápagos is part of Ecuador — but there are extra steps. The UK government says you need evidence of a hotel booking or an invitation letter, a return flight to the mainland, a Transit Control Card bought at your departure airport before check-in, and travel health insurance, which is mandatory for foreign tourists. Tourists can stay up to 60 days. The islands' protected areas also charge an entrance fee.
entries.note: Rewritten to the UK entry requirements; the bag-screening claim and the USD 20 and USD 200 amounts could not be confirmed.

entries.old: The US dollar — Ecuador dollarised in 2000 and uses US notes alongside Ecuadorian coins of the same value. Bring plenty of small denominations; USD 50 and 100 notes are frequently refused outside big hotels.
entries.new: The US dollar. The UK government says US dollars and the 5, 10, 25 and 50 centavo coins minted in Ecuador are the only legal currencies. Australia's Smartraveller advises carrying US$1 notes, as many smaller shops and taxi drivers don't change large notes.
entries.note: The year of dollarisation and the claim that USD 50 and 100 notes are refused had no source.

entries.old: widely-in-cities
entries.new: limited
entries.note: Canada's travel advice says cards are accepted in larger stores and for larger purchases but many merchants take only cash; 'widely in cities' overstated it.

entries.old: Cards work in hotels, resort restaurants and larger shops, but Egypt runs on cash: bazaars, taxis, site entrance extras and tips (baksheesh) all need small notes. ATMs are common in cities and resorts. Carry small-denomination pounds.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says major credit cards are accepted in larger stores and for larger purchases, but many merchants accept only cash or charge a fee for card payment. It adds that US dollars are preferred, particularly at tourist sites, and that some travel agents and tour operators ask for payment in US cash only.
entries.note: Model-written text (ATMs common, baksheesh) replaced with what Canada's travel advice says.

entries.old: October to April brings mild, sunny weather ideal for the pyramids and Nile Valley sites; summer is extremely hot inland, though Red Sea resorts stay busy year-round.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Egypt. Canada's travel advice notes that sand and dust storms can occur in spring, and that heavy rains can cause flooding in low-lying areas of northern Egypt.
entries.note: No official seasonal guidance found; climate claims withdrawn, Canada's climate notes kept.

entries.old: Drones are banned in Egypt without a hard-to-get military permit — do not bring one, even packed away; they are confiscated and travelers have been detained.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says you must not import, use or produce drones in Egypt without prior permission from the Egyptian Ministry of Defence; doing so without permission can bring a prison sentence of up to 7 years or a fine of 5,000 to 50,000 Egyptian pounds.
entries.note: Drone rule restated as the UK FCDO gives it (Ministry of Defence permission; penalties); 'travelers have been detained' unsupported.

entries.old: Exporting antiquities or anything that looks like one is a serious criminal offense. Buy souvenirs from licensed shops and keep receipts.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says it is prohibited to export any antiquity or any item older than 100 years without a licence.
entries.note: Restated as Canada gives it (antiquities and items over 100 years old need an export licence); shopping advice unsupported.

entries.old: Satellite phones and some radio equipment require prior authorization.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says officials are likely to confiscate satellite phones or radio communications equipment unless you have prior clearance from the Ministry of Telecommunications, and that high-value electronic devices and recording equipment should be declared on arrival.
entries.note: Restated as the UK FCDO gives it; 'some radio equipment requires prior authorization' replaced with the FCDO's wording.

entries.old: Apply for the Egyptian eVisa only at the official portal visa2egypt.gov.eg — look-alike sites charge large markups on the 30 USD fee and sometimes deliver nothing.
entries.new: Apply for the Egyptian eVisa at the official portal visa2egypt.gov.eg. The UK government's travel advice says you do not need to buy a visa from an agent at the airport: agents often charge more than the 30 US dollar fee, and harassment by an agent can be reported to the tourist police in the terminal.
entries.note: Claims about look-alike sites are unsupported; replaced with the FCDO's advice on airport visa agents.

entries.old: Drones are illegal to bring into Egypt without a military permit, even packed in luggage. They are confiscated at the airport and can lead to detention.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says drones may not be imported or used in Egypt without prior permission from the Ministry of Defence, with penalties of up to 7 years in prison or a fine of 5,000 to 50,000 Egyptian pounds.
entries.note: Confiscation and detention claims unsupported; restated per FCDO.

entries.old: Flying directly to Sharm El Sheikh, Dahab, Nuweiba or Taba and staying in South Sinai? You can get a free 15-day Sinai-only entry stamp instead of a visa, but it does not cover Cairo, Luxor or diving trips to Ras Mohammed by boat, so most excursion-takers still buy the full visa.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says that if you arrive by air at Sharm El-Sheikh and stay less than 15 days at the resorts of Sharm El Sheikh, Dahab, Nuweiba or Taba, you get a free entry permission stamp and need no visa. To travel outside those resorts or stay longer than 15 days you need a visa, available at Sharm El-Sheikh Airport or online.
entries.note: Restated per FCDO (arrival by air at Sharm El-Sheikh); the Ras Mohammed boat-trip claim is unsupported.

entries.old: Never photograph military installations, checkpoints or bridges — cameras and phones can be seized. Small tips (baksheesh) are a routine part of daily life for guides, drivers and washroom attendants; keep 5–20 EGP notes handy.
entries.new: It is illegal to take photos of, or near, military property in Egypt, including the Suez Canal, according to the UK government's travel advice. Canada's travel advice adds that photographing bridges, canals, government, police and embassy buildings and vehicles, and military personnel is prohibited.
entries.note: Photography rule restated per FCDO and Canada; baksheesh amounts and seizure claims unsupported and removed.

entries.old: Travelers arriving directly at Sharm El Sheikh, Taba or other South Sinai airports can get a free entry stamp allowing 15 days in the South Sinai resorts (Sharm, Dahab, Nuweiba, Taba) without a visa. It does not allow travel to Cairo, Luxor or the rest of Egypt — for that you need the regular 30-day visa.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says that if you arrive by air at Sharm El-Sheikh and stay less than 15 days at the resorts of Sharm El Sheikh, Dahab, Nuweiba or Taba, you get a free entry permission stamp on arrival and need no visa. It does not cover travel outside those resorts or a stay longer than 15 days — for that you need a visa, available at Sharm El-Sheikh Airport or online.
entries.note: The stamp applies to arrival by air at Sharm El-Sheikh per FCDO; 'Taba or other South Sinai airports' unsupported.

entries.old: At least 6 months from your date of arrival. Airlines enforce this at check-in, so renew your passport first if you are close to the limit.
entries.new: At least 6 months from your date of arrival.
entries.note: Unsupported sentence about airline check-in enforcement deleted.

entries.new: Canada's travel advice says you may need to declare all currency you carry on arrival and departure, and that import and export limits may apply.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice states; confiscation and wildlife-export claims are not in an official source.

entries.old: Do not photograph the presidential palace, airports, ports, checkpoints or anything military or governmental. The rules are enforced and cameras or phones can be confiscated; ask permission before photographing people.
entries.new: Do not photograph government or military buildings or airports — the UK FCDO says it is illegal and you could be arrested and detained. Ask permission before photographing people.
entries.note: Confiscation claim replaced with what UK FCDO advice states.

entries.old: Carry your passport (or a certified copy) and visa at all times — police checkpoints are frequent on Bioko and the mainland, and missing documents commonly lead to fines or lengthy delays.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says to carry your passport or residence permit (or copies) throughout the country: police and military roadblocks are common, and failing to show identification on request can lead to arrest and detention.
entries.note: Rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Is Equatorial Guinea really that hard to visit? — It was long ranked among the world's most difficult destinations — few embassies, demanding paperwork and discretionary refusals. The online e-visa the UK FCDO describes makes applying easier, but expect more documentation than usual (hotel booking, bank statements, sometimes police clearance) and allow plenty of time.

Tobacco limits depend on the country, and travellers under 17 get no alcohol or tobacco allowance.

entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Eswatini. Canada's travel advice says the rainy season extends from October to April, when some roads may become hazardous.

entries.old: Cards are accepted at major hotels and a growing number of venues in Addis Ababa, but Ethiopia remains overwhelmingly a cash economy. Carry birr outside the capital and expect ATMs to be unreliable up-country.
entries.new: The UK Foreign Office describes Ethiopia as a cash-based society: card payments and ATMs are limited and unreliable, especially outside cities, so get enough cash before leaving them.
entries.note: Rewritten to what the cited official source says.

entries.old: October to March is the dry season — clear skies for the Simien Mountains, Lalibela and the historic north; the main rains fall from June to September.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season normally runs from June to September, when seasonal flooding can hamper overland travel and mudslides and landslides can make roads impassable.
entries.note: Rewritten to the climate statement the cited source makes.

entries.old: Drones may not be brought into Ethiopia without prior authorization from the civil aviation authority — undeclared drones are confiscated at the airport.

entries.old: Exchange money only through banks and licensed bureaux and keep the receipts — street exchange is illegal.
entries.new: (removed or rewritten)

entries.old: Addis Ababa sits at about 2,355 m and the northern highlands are higher still. Take it easy for the first day or two and drink plenty of water.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Addis Ababa is about 2,500 m above sea level and that high-altitude illness may occur. Take it easy for the first day or two and drink plenty of water.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: Ethiopia uses its own calendar (seven to eight years behind the Gregorian one) and counts the hours from dawn — always confirm whether a time or date is "Ethiopian" or "European" when booking.
entries.new: (removed)

entries.old: Change money only at banks and licensed bureaux and keep every receipt. You will need them to convert leftover birr back, and unofficial exchange can land you in serious trouble.
entries.new: Change money only at banks or official foreign exchange offices and keep every receipt: the UK Foreign Office says that without one you are unlikely to be able to change leftover birr back, and Canada says black-market exchange is illegal.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: A certificate is only demanded if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Vaccination is nonetheless widely recommended for travel outside Addis Ababa, along with routine travel vaccines. Check with a travel clinic.
entries.new: A certificate is only demanded if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Ask a travel clinic whether vaccination is advisable for your itinerary, along with routine travel vaccines.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources say, attributed.

entries.new: false
entries.note: No official source found that states tap water in Fiji is safe to drink; withdrawn to false.

entries.old: …Once you reach the Yasawas, Lomaiviti or a village stay it turns cash-only…
entries.new: Cards accepted by most hotels, restaurants and shops; ATMs in main centres and some rural areas (Government of Canada).
entries.note: Island-by-island cash-only claims are not stated by any official source read.

entries.old: May to October is the dry season — lower humidity, clear water for diving and no cyclone risk. November to April is hotter and wetter, with the cyclone season running roughly November 1 to April 30; it is also cheaper and greener.
entries.new: The Government of Canada says the rainy and cyclone season runs from November to April, and the UK Foreign Office notes that cyclones can occur throughout the year, bringing strong winds, heavy rain, flooding and landslides.
entries.note: "No cyclone risk" from May to October contradicts the UK FCDO, which says cyclones occur throughout the year.

entries.new: ["The UK Foreign Office says Fiji customs has strict quarantine regulations: officers X-ray all luggage arriving at Nadi airport and confiscate most fresh foodstuffs, unless you are arriving from a country with a quarantine agreement with Fiji."]

entries.old: Cards and contactless payments are accepted virtually everywhere in Finland, including buses, kiosks and market stalls. Many places are card-only, and cash is rarely needed.
entries.new: No official source we could read describes how widely cards are accepted in Finland. Canada's travel advice notes that the currency is the euro (EUR) and that EUR 10,000 or more must be declared to customs when entering or leaving the EU.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: June–August offers the midnight sun, lakeside cottages and warm city terraces; December–March is the season for Lapland, husky safaris and the northern lights.
entries.new: No official source we checked gives seasonal guidance for Finland; the months shown are not an official recommendation.
entries.note: No official seasonal guidance found.

entries.old: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea). | No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.
entries.new: Arriving from outside the EU, the EU's Your Europe portal lists duty-free allowances of 200 cigarettes, 1 litre of spirits over 22% and other goods worth up to €300 (€430 for air and sea travellers). | Between EU countries, no further duty is due on goods for your own use once tax has been paid where you bought them, though EU countries may set indicative guideline quantities for tobacco and alcohol.
entries.note: Only what an official source states is kept, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: For Lapland in winter, pack for -20°C or colder — layered thermal clothing, insulated boots and a proper hat; tour operators often lend thermal suits, but everyday gear is your own responsibility.
entries.new: For Lapland in winter, pack layered thermal clothing, insulated boots and a proper hat.

entries.old: Do not bother exchanging much cash — Finland is close to cashless, and some cafés and buses accept cards or mobile payments only.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports it.

entries.old: The aurora season in Finnish Lapland runs roughly from late August to April, with the best odds on clear, dark nights between December and March away from city lights. No special permits are needed, just warm clothing.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports it.

entries.old: Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere, including bakeries and taxis. Some cafés apply a small card minimum, so a little cash is handy.
entries.new: No official source we checked describes card acceptance in France specifically. The European Central Bank's 2024 payments survey found that across the euro area 89% of in-store transactions were, or could have been, paid without cash, and 95% could be paid in cash.
entries.note: The bakery, taxi and card-minimum claims had no official source; replaced with the ECB euro-area survey.

entries.old: April–June and September–October offer mild weather and thinner crowds; July–August is peak season, and many Paris businesses close in August while the coast fills up.
entries.new: No official source we checked gives seasonal guidance for France; the months shown are not an official recommendation. The UK government says there is a high risk of wildfires in the summer season from April to October.
entries.note: The crowd and August-closure claims had no official source.

entries.old: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea). | No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.
entries.new: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea). | Goods for your own use bought in another EU country carry no further duty. Above the EU guide levels (for example 800 cigarettes or 10 litres of spirits), customs may ask you to show they are for personal use.
entries.note: EU rules: personal-use goods are not unlimited — customs may check quantities above the EU guide levels.

entries.old: Pickpocketing and distraction scams (petitions, gold rings, friendship bracelets) are common on the Paris metro and around major sights. Keep valuables zipped away.
entries.new: The UK government says thieves and pickpockets operate on the Paris Métro, on RER lines and at mainline stations, sometimes in gangs where one person distracts you. Keep your passport, cards and valuables in separate bags or pockets.
entries.note: The named scams (petitions, gold rings, bracelets) had no official source.

entries.old: Transport strikes (grèves) periodically disrupt trains, the metro and flights. Check SNCF and airport status before travel days and build in slack.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says strikes occur regularly, particularly in transport, and Australia's Smartraveller says they can affect trains and flights. Check the status of your trains and flights before travel days and build in slack.
entries.note: Attributed to the Canadian and Australian advice.
Police 177 confirmed by Canada and the UK FCDO. Fire '18' is stated by neither (Canada lists only full Libreville and Port-Gentil fire-station numbers) and was withdrawn.

entries.old: Cards are accepted at larger hotels and supermarkets in Libreville and Port-Gentil, but Gabon is overwhelmingly a cash economy. Carry CFA francs, especially outside the main cities.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says credit cards are accepted only in Libreville's large hotels, restaurants and supermarkets, that ATMs are available but cash withdrawals are limited, and to use cash for all transactions if possible. Euros and US dollars are widely accepted, though high exchange charges may apply. The UK government's travel advice says credit cards are not widely accepted except at hotels.
entries.note: Enums confirmed (limited / high). Text rewritten to what Canada and the UK FCDO say; Port-Gentil card acceptance was not stated by either.

entries.old: {"months": [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], "text": "The long dry season from late May to September is the best window for Loango and the national parks — cooler, drier and with easier road access."}
entries.new: {"months": [6, 7, 8, 9], "text": "Canada's travel advice says Gabon's rainy seasons run from October to mid-December and from mid-February to May, when some roads outside urban areas may be impassable. No official source we could read names a best time to visit."}
entries.note: May is inside the rainy season Canada gives (mid-February to May), so the months now cover June–September only; park-access claims withdrawn.

entries.old: Exporting ivory, wildlife trophies or protected animal and plant products is prohibited without CITES permits. | Large amounts of CFA franc cash are subject to BEAC currency-control rules. Declare significant sums on arrival and departure.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says there are strict rules about goods you can take into or out of Gabon, and that you must declare anything that may be prohibited or subject to tax or duty.
entries.note: The CITES/ivory and BEAC currency-control notes are not stated by any official source read; replaced with the FCDO's general customs advice.

entries.old: The yellow fever certificate is checked on arrival — travelers without a valid yellow card can be refused entry or vaccinated on the spot.
entries.new: You must have a certificate proving yellow fever vaccination to enter Gabon, according to the UK government's travel advice. Carry it with your passport.
entries.note: Refusal or on-the-spot vaccination is not stated by an official source; restated as the FCDO gives it.

entries.old: Withdraw CFA francs in Libreville before traveling — ATMs are scarce and unreliable outside the capital and Port-Gentil, and cards are rarely accepted upcountry.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says credit cards are accepted only in Libreville's large hotels, restaurants and supermarkets, and that ATMs are available but cash withdrawals are limited — so use cash for transactions where you can.
entries.note: Restated per Canada; the Port-Gentil and 'unreliable ATMs' claims are unsupported.

entries.old: Visits to Loango, Lopé and other national parks need advance planning — internal flights, boats and park guides are limited and best booked through a lodge or operator.
entries.new: (deleted)
entries.note: No official source describes park logistics, flights or guides; tip withdrawn.

entries.old: Avoid photographing government buildings, the port, airports and anything military. It can lead to questioning or confiscation of your camera.
entries.new: Photography of government and military buildings and airports is illegal in Gabon and may lead to arrest, according to the UK government's travel advice.
entries.note: Restated per FCDO; the port is not named by the source.

entries.old: The Central African CFA franc (XAF), shared with Cameroon, Congo, Chad, the Central African Republic and Equatorial Guinea. Cash dominates outside the biggest hotels, so carry francs — euros are the easiest currency to exchange.
entries.new: The Central African CFA franc (XAF). Canada's travel advice says euros and US dollars are widely accepted, though high exchange charges may apply, and that credit cards are accepted only in Libreville's large hotels, restaurants and supermarkets.
entries.note: The list of countries sharing the currency and 'euros are easiest to exchange' are unsupported; restated per Canada.

Beach and birdwatching claims withdrawn; rainy-season dates kept.

entries.old: true
entries.new: false
entries.note: The UK FCDO lists varying water quality as a health risk in Georgia and notes that bottled water is widely available.

entries.old: Duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes and 4 liters of alcoholic beverages per adult.
entries.new: The Revenue Service of Georgia allows travellers aged 18 or over to bring in duty-free, once per 30 days: 200 cigarettes (or 50 cigars, 50 cigarillos or 250 g of other tobacco), and 1 litre of drinks of 22% or more (or 2 litres under 22%) plus 4 litres of wine.
entries.note: Alcohol allowance corrected to the Revenue Service of Georgia; medicines note rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Medicines for personal use are fine in reasonable quantities; strong opioid painkillers require documentation.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says Georgia has a very strict anti-drugs policy that covers some medicines: non-prescription medicines containing codeine are illegal, and prescription medicine must travel with a doctor's prescription and in its original packaging. Check a specific medicine with the Revenue Service of Georgia or a Georgian embassy.
entries.note: Alcohol allowance corrected to the Revenue Service of Georgia; medicines note rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Never enter Abkhazia or South Ossetia from the Russian side — entering Georgia through these occupied regions is a criminal offense under Georgian law and can mean fines or imprisonment when you cross into government-controlled territory. Approaching the boundary lines is also risky.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says it is illegal under Georgian law to enter Georgia from Russia through South Ossetia or Abkhazia, with heavy fines or up to 4 years in prison. It advises against all travel to both regions and all but essential travel next to their boundary lines, which are generally unmarked.
entries.note: Rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Georgia is the world's oldest wine region — 8,000 vintages of qvevri (clay-vessel) winemaking, UNESCO-listed. Base yourself in Sighnaghi or Telavi for the Kakheti wine route, and try amber (skin-contact) wines at family wineries.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: Wine-heritage and itinerary claims are not stated by an official source.

entries.old: Mountain roads to Kazbegi, Svaneti and especially Tusheti (the Abano Pass) are narrow, unpaved in stretches and weather-dependent. Hire a local 4x4 driver rather than self-driving, and expect closures outside June–October.
entries.new: The UK FCDO warns that roads outside city centres are often badly lit and poor, and that heavy rain, flooding and snow at higher altitudes can make travel difficult or impossible in remote areas. Make sure your vehicle is suitable for off-road driving and check weather conditions locally.
entries.note: Route-specific closure claims removed; rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Tap water is safe to drink in Tbilisi and most towns. It comes from mountain sources; in remote villages or after heavy rain, bottled water is a sensible fallback.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: Contradicted by the UK FCDO, which lists varying water quality as a health risk.

entries.old: A full 365 days per entry for the roughly 90 nationalities on the visa-free list, including the US, UK, all EU states, Canada, Australia, Japan, Ukraine, Turkey and Russia. It is one of the most generous visa-free allowances in the world, which is why Georgia is popular with remote workers.
entries.new: A full 365 days per entry for the roughly 90 nationalities on the visa-free list, including the US, UK, all EU states, Canada, Australia, Japan, Ukraine, Turkey and Russia.

entries.old: Bring all the money you need as cash, ideally euros. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro and exchange in Bissau is straightforward, while ATMs and card payments cannot be relied on.
entries.new: Bring the cash you need: the UK government says credit cards are rarely used and there are not many ATMs, and Canada says there are none. Canada also says local currency may not be imported or exported, while foreign currency must be declared on arrival.

entries.old: Guinea-Bissau has a long history of coups and political crises. Avoid protests, checkpoints arguments and the areas around government and military buildings, and monitor the news during your stay.

The UK government advises avoiding sensitive areas such as military installations and government buildings and following local authorities during any unrest.

Australia's Smartraveller reports heightened political and social tensions, including in Conakry, that may deteriorate without warning, and Canada's travel advice says to avoid areas where demonstrations and large gatherings take place.

Baggage allowances are strict — often around 20 lb (9 kg) — and flights are weather-dependent, so leave a buffer day before an international connection.

entries.old: Even visa-free visitors are given a specific number of days by the officer at the desk — often 30 rather than the full allowance. Check the stamp before you leave the counter and apply to the Central Immigration and Passport Office in Georgetown if you need longer; overstaying brings fines and delays at departure.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says visitors can normally stay for 30 days and can apply to Guyana's immigration support services for one-month extensions. Overstaying can lead to arrest, a one-year prison sentence, a fine of up to 50,000 Guyana dollars and deportation at your own expense. Canada's travel advice says to make sure your passport is stamped on arrival.

entries.old: Carry your yellow fever certificate with your passport. It is checked if you arrive from a risk country, and Brazil, Suriname and several onward destinations ask for it from travelers who have been in Guyana.
entries.new: Carry your yellow fever certificate with your passport: you must show it if you arrive from a country with a risk of yellow fever transmission, and Canada's travel advice notes there is a risk of yellow fever in Guyana itself.

entries.old: Guyana rewards care rather than nerve. Violent and armed robbery is a real risk in parts of Georgetown, so avoid walking after dark, use booked taxis, and keep valuables out of sight. The interior — Kaieteur, Iwokrama, the Rupununi — is very safe from crime but genuinely remote, with limited medical help, so travel with an established operator and insurance that covers evacuation.

Canada's travel advice says travel to the interior is not safe because of low police presence, and the FCDO says medical facilities are very limited, even in Georgetown.

Tobacco limits depend on the country, and travellers under 17 get no alcohol or tobacco allowance.

entries.old: No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.
entries.new: Between EU countries, alcohol and tobacco bought with tax paid, for your own use and not for resale, owe no further tax, according to the EU's Your Europe portal.

entries.old: In Budapest use only official yellow taxis with a company logo and fixed government tariff, or apps like Bolt and Főtaxi — freelance taxis hailed near sights and clubs are known for heavy overcharging.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official page we could read supports this.

entries.old: At thermal baths (Széchenyi, Gellért, Rudas) bring a swimsuit, towel and flip-flops; a swim cap is required only in swimming-lap pools. Lockers and cabins are included or rentable. Book popular baths online in high season.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official page we could read supports this.

entries.old: safe
entries.new: not stated
entries.note: No official source we could read states whether tap water is safe to drink; the value is now shown as not stated.

entries.old: Iceland is effectively cashless. Cards and contactless payments are accepted everywhere, from fuel pumps and buses to remote guesthouses. There is no need to withdraw krónur for a normal visit.
entries.new: No official source we could read describes card acceptance in Iceland.
entries.note: Withdrawn: the 'effectively cashless' claims had no official source.

entries.old: June–August brings the midnight sun, open highland roads and the best hiking; September and February–March offer good northern-lights odds with milder crowds — winter travel needs flexible plans around storms.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Iceland. Canada's travel advice says roads in the highlands and other remote areas are open only in summer, and that winter tires are mandatory between November and April.
entries.note: Withdrawn: the midnight-sun and northern-lights claims had no official source.

entries.old: ["Strict biosecurity rules: raw meat and unpasteurised dairy from outside the EEA may not be brought in, and used riding, angling and hunting gear must be disinfected and certified before arrival.", "Alcohol allowances are limited and strictly enforced. Many arrivals use the duty-free store in Keflavík airport, where prices are far below city retail."]
entries.new: ["Iceland Revenue and Customs says visitors may bring in duty-free up to 10 kg of food worth no more than ISK 25,000, but no meat or dairy products from outside the European Economic Area.", "The duty-free alcohol allowance is a set of combinations, for example 1 litre of spirits, 0.75 litre of wine and 3 litres of beer, or 18 litres of beer; the tobacco allowance is 200 cigarettes or 250 g of other tobacco. You must be 20 to bring in alcohol and 18 for tobacco.", "Angling gear and riding clothing used abroad must be disinfected, with a certificate from an authorised veterinary officer or at your own cost on arrival; used leather riding gear such as saddles and bridles may not be imported."]
entries.note: Rewritten to Iceland Revenue and Customs; the airport duty-free price claim had no official source.

entries.old: Weather can turn dangerous within hours … never drive marked F-roads without a suitable 4x4 …
entries.new: FCDO / Canada road advice
entries.note: Rewritten to what the FCDO and Canada state.

entries.old: Gravel chips, sandstorms and wind-torn car doors are the classic rental-car claims …
entries.new: FCDO weather-damage warning
entries.note: Rewritten to the FCDO's wording.

entries.new: (removed)

entries.old: Main roads are kept open but storms close them at short notice …
entries.new: Canada winter-driving advice

entries.old: general: 112 · police: 100 · ambulance: 102
entries.new: general: 112 · police: 100 · ambulance: 102 · fire: 101
entries.note: Emergency numbers read from official travel advice; numbers no source states were removed.

entries.old: Cards work in hotels, malls and city restaurants; small shops, rickshaws and rural areas are cash-first. UPI dominates local payments — foreign visitors can register for UPI with some providers.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says non-residents are prohibited from importing or exporting Indian rupees. No official source we could read describes card acceptance.
entries.note: Rewritten to what the cited official source says.

entries.old: October to March is dry and comfortable across most of the country; the Himalayan north is best May–September.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the monsoon season runs from June to September, when heavy rain can cause flooding and landslides across the country.
entries.note: Rewritten to the climate statement the cited source makes.

entries.old: Satellite phones are prohibited without a license; drones require prior permission.
entries.new: (removed or rewritten)
entries.note: Not stated by an official source we could read; removed or replaced with what the source says.

entries.old: Some regions (parts of the northeast, Andaman & Nicobar tribal areas, border zones) require special permits beyond your visa.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says special permits are required to visit parts of India designated as restricted or protected areas; India's Bureau of Immigration lists them.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: Drink only bottled or purified water and ease into street food — stomach upsets are the most common traveler ailment.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says travellers' diarrhoea is the most common illness affecting travellers. Its rule of thumb: boil it, cook it, peel it, or leave it.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: {"general": "112", "police": "110", "ambulance": "119", "fire": "113"}
entries.new: {"police": "110", "ambulance": "118", "fire": "112"}
entries.note: The UK Foreign Office lists ambulance 118, fire 112 and police 110. The previously published ambulance 119, fire 113 and "general" 112 labels are not stated by any official source read, so the list now follows the FCDO.

entries.old: Cards are fine in city hotels, malls and tourist restaurants; markets, warungs, ferries and rural areas run on cash. The local QRIS QR standard is spreading fast but usually needs an Indonesian payment app.
entries.new: The Government of Canada says credit cards are not widely accepted outside large urban centres and tourist areas, and advises carrying cash when visiting remote areas. The UK Foreign Office warns that credit card fraud is common and advises using only licensed money changers, identified by a Bank Indonesia logo and a QR code.
entries.note: The QRIS claim and the list of cash-only places are not stated by any official source read; text limited to the Canadian and UK statements.

entries.old: May to September is the dry season across Java, Bali and most of the archipelago — the best window for beaches, diving and volcano hikes.
entries.new: The UK Foreign Office says the rainy season usually runs from October to March, but in Eastern Indonesia the wet season usually runs from April to August; wildfires and smoke haze are worst in the dry season, usually April to September. The Government of Canada notes that heavy rain is common throughout the year.
entries.note: No official source gives a best season; the text now states the seasons the FCDO gives, including the different wet season in Eastern Indonesia.

entries.old: Duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes and 1 liter of alcohol per adult; excess alcohol is confiscated.
entries.new: Indonesian customs allows each passenger personal goods worth up to USD 500 duty-free; each adult may also bring at most 200 cigarettes, 25 cigars or 100 g of tobacco, and 1 liter of alcoholic drink. Excess excise goods are destroyed by officers.
entries.note: Allowance confirmed on the customs site; it adds the USD 500 personal-goods exemption and the cigar/tobacco alternatives, and says excess is destroyed (not confiscated).

entries.old: Narcotics offenses carry the death penalty. Some prescription drugs (including codeine and sleeping pills) need documentation.
entries.new: The UK Foreign Office warns that possessing, using, making or trafficking illegal drugs can bring long prison sentences or the death penalty, and that all cannabis products, including CBD, are illegal. The Government of Canada notes that medicines containing morphine or codeine are controlled substances in Indonesia and cannot be brought in without prior permission from the Ministry of Health.
entries.note: "Sleeping pills" is not stated by any official source read; the medicines claim now follows the Government of Canada (morphine, codeine; Ministry of Health permission).

entries.new: police 110 · ambulance 115 · fire 125

entries.old: safe to drink
entries.new: not for drinking
entries.note: Australia's Smartraveller advises boiled or bottled water.

entries.old: Foreign bank cards do not work in Iran because of sanctions. Bring everything you need in cash (euros or US dollars) and exchange gradually, or load a prepaid local tourist card. Prices are often quoted in tomans: 1 toman = 10 rials.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Iran's economy is exclusively cash-based: credit cards are not accepted and ATMs serve only local bank accounts. The UK government adds that non-Iranian debit cards will not work, that changing money on the street is illegal, and that euros and US dollars are more commonly accepted at exchange offices than pounds sterling.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: Spring (March–May) and fall (September–November) are ideal for Tehran, Isfahan, Shiraz and Yazd; summers are fiercely hot in the center and south.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the weather is very dry and hot from May to October, when dust storms can occur, and that the rainy season runs from November to March, sometimes with flash flooding.
entries.note: Replaced with the climate statement the cited source supports.

entries.old: Alcohol is illegal in Iran and may not be imported under any circumstances. | Drones and satellite communication devices are confiscated and can lead to arrest. Leave them at home. | Any evidence of travel to Israel in your passport will lead to refusal of entry.
entries.new: The UK government says it is illegal to import, sell, manufacture or drink alcohol in Iran, and that importing pork products is illegal. | The UK government says you need permission from the Iranian authorities to import or use drones or satellite phones; using them without permission is illegal and can lead to arrest. | Canada's travel advice says travellers have been denied entry because their passports bore an Israeli visa or border stamp, or an Egyptian or Jordanian stamp from a crossing on the border with Israel.
entries.note: Only what an official source states is kept, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: Women, including foreign visitors, are legally required to cover their hair with a headscarf in public and to wear loose clothing covering arms and legs; men should avoid shorts. Enforcement varies, but the law applies from the moment you board an Iran-bound flight.
entries.new: The UK government says Islamic dress codes are strictly enforced: in public, women must cover their heads with a headscarf and wear trousers or a floor-length skirt with a long-sleeved tunic or coat reaching mid-thigh or knee, and men should wear long trousers and long-sleeved shirts.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Iran does not recognize dual nationality — dual citizens, especially Iranian dual nationals, have been detained and cannot receive consular help. Many governments explicitly advise dual nationals not to travel.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller says Iran does not recognise dual nationality and that foreign and dual nationals are at high risk of arbitrary detention or arrest, without guaranteed consular access. Many governments advise dual nationals not to travel.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Budget your whole trip in cash before arrival — euros are easiest to exchange — and change money at licensed exchange offices (sarrafi), which give far better rates than banks.
entries.new: Bring your whole budget in cash. The UK government says non-Iranian debit cards will not work, changing money on the street is illegal, and exchange offices accept euros and US dollars more readily than pounds sterling.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: No. International card networks do not operate in Iran because of sanctions. Bring your entire budget in cash (euros or dollars are best) or arrange a prepaid Iranian tourist debit card through your tour operator.
entries.new: No. Canada's travel advice says the economy is exclusively cash-based, credit cards are not accepted and ATMs serve only local bank accounts; the UK government adds that non-Iranian debit cards will not work. Bring your budget in cash, preferably US dollars or euros.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: By law women must cover their hair with a headscarf and wear loose clothing that covers the arms and legs. A long tunic or manteau over trousers is standard. In practice enforcement fluctuates and dress in the big cities is fairly relaxed, but the requirement remains law for visitors too.
entries.new: The UK government says Islamic dress codes are strictly enforced. In public places women must cover their heads with a headscarf and wear trousers or a floor-length skirt with a long-sleeved tunic or coat reaching mid-thigh or knee, and may be asked to wear a chador at religious sites. It also reports that the authorities have arrested and detained women for not following the dress code, and that enforcement crackdowns can happen at any time.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Street crime is low and travelers consistently report warm hospitality, but many governments — including the US, UK and Canada — advise against all travel because of the risk of arbitrary detention and regional tensions. Dual nationals face particular risk. Weigh the advisories seriously and keep insurance and registration in order if you go.
entries.new: Many governments advise against all travel. Australia's Smartraveller says do not travel to Iran and that foreigners, including dual nationals, are at high risk of arbitrary detention or arrest; the UK government says British and British-Iranian dual nationals face a very high risk of arrest, detention and questioning. Weigh the advisories seriously and keep insurance and registration in order if you go.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.new: {"police": "911", "ambulance": "122", "fire": "115"}
entries.note: The UK government lists 911 for police, not 104.

entries.old: Iraq is overwhelmingly cash-based. Bring US dollars (newer, undamaged notes) to exchange. Cards work only at a handful of upmarket hotels, and ATMs accepting foreign cards are scarce, though somewhat better in Erbil.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Iraq's economy is primarily cash-based, US dollars are accepted in some shops, and you may have difficulty finding an ATM that accepts an international card. Australia's Smartraveller says US dollars and euros are the easiest foreign currencies to exchange at banks and exchange bureaus.
entries.note: Rewritten to Canada's and Australia's advice; the Erbil ATM and note-condition claims had no source.
Canada describes May to October as very dry and hot.

entries.old: Spring (March–April) and fall (October–November) avoid the ferocious summer, when temperatures can pass 50°C in Baghdad and the south.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the weather is very dry and hot from May to October, and Australia's Smartraveller says daytime temperatures can exceed 50°C from July to September; sand and dust storms are common in spring and summer. No official source names a best season.
entries.note: Replaced with the climate statements in the Canadian and Australian advice.

entries.old: Photography near checkpoints, government buildings and military sites is dangerous — always ask before photographing people or infrastructure. | Drones are effectively prohibited and will be confiscated. | Evidence of travel to Israel can lead to refusal of entry.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller says it is illegal to photograph or film government buildings, checkpoints, military bases and embassies, and that you need approval to film in a public place. | Australia's Smartraveller says people flying drones without permission have been detained. | Australia's Smartraveller says the authorities may refuse entry if your passport contains Israeli stamps or visas; Canada says such passports face additional screening before an Iraqi visa is issued.
entries.note: Attributed to Australia's and Canada's advice; 'drones will be confiscated' became 'flyers have been detained', as Australia says.

entries.old: Bring your budget in US dollars cash, in good condition — older or marked notes are refused. The e-Visa itself is paid online when you apply, not in cash at the airport.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Iraq's economy is primarily cash-based and ATMs that accept international cards are hard to find, so bring enough cash; Australia's Smartraveller says US dollars and euros are the easiest to exchange. The e-Visa itself is paid online when you apply.
entries.note: The claim that older or marked notes are refused had no source.

entries.old: Expect frequent checkpoints between cities. Carry your passport at all times, keep visa copies on your phone, and build waiting time into any road journey.
entries.new: The UK government says it is a legal requirement to carry photographic ID in Iraq and that the authorities stop people for ID checks at checkpoints within cities and on main roads. Always carry your passport and keep copies of your visa.
entries.note: Attributed to the UK government.

entries.old: During Ashura and the Arbaeen pilgrimage, Karbala and Najaf receive millions of visitors — accommodation sells out and roads close. Dress conservatively at all religious sites year-round.
entries.new: The UK government says the Arba'een pilgrimage attracts millions of pilgrims to Iraq and usually falls between August and September; Canada put the 2026 pilgrimage around 3 August and notes a heightened security risk. The UK advises following local dress codes.
entries.note: The Ashura, accommodation and road-closure claims had no source.

entries.old: Iraq remains a high-risk destination: most governments advise against all travel, or against all nonessential travel because of terrorism, kidnapping and unrest. That said, organized tourism to Baghdad, Babylon, the southern shrine cities and especially the Kurdistan Region has grown since 2021. Go with an experienced operator, expect checkpoints, and follow advisories.
entries.new: No. Canada and Australia advise against all travel to Iraq, and the UK advises against all travel to large parts of the country, including Kirkuk, Ninawa and Salah al-Din provinces, and against all but essential travel to much of the rest. Missile, drone and rocket attacks have struck locations in Iraq, including the Kurdistan Region. Check your government's advice before considering a trip.
entries.note: The claim that organised tourism has grown since 2021 had no source; Canada and Australia now advise against all travel.

entries.old: No. Israeli passport holders are not admitted to Iraq, and Iraqi law criminalises contact that would normalise relations. Evidence of travel to Israel in another passport can also cause problems at the border.
entries.new: No. Israeli passport holders are not admitted to Iraq. Australia's Smartraveller says the authorities may also refuse entry if your passport contains Israeli stamps or visas.
entries.note: The claim about an Iraqi law criminalising normalisation had no source here.

entries.new: ["Irish", "English"]
entries.note: Confirmed. Reordered as Article 8 of the Constitution has it: Irish is the first official language, English a second official language.

entries.note: No official source describes card or contactless acceptance; text withdrawn and cardsAccepted set conservatively.

entries.old: May to September brings the mildest weather and up to 17 hours of daylight in midsummer, but pack rain gear whatever the month; Irish weather changes by the hour.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Ireland. Canada's travel advice notes that Ireland is subject to seasonal storms, windstorms and severe weather, and that heavy rains can cause flooding.
entries.note: Daylight and seasonal claims withdrawn; Canada's climate note kept.

entries.old: Arriving from outside the EU: duty-free allowance of 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits (or 4 liters of wine), and other goods up to €430 per adult arriving by air or sea.
entries.new: Arriving from outside the EU, Revenue's duty-free allowances are goods worth up to €430 if you are 15 or over (€215 if under 15), plus 200 cigarettes (or 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco), 1 litre of spirits or 2 litres of drinks up to 22% alcohol, 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer.
entries.note: Corrected from Revenue: wine (4 L) and beer (16 L) are separate allowances on top of spirits, not an alternative to them, and the €430 figure applies to travellers aged 15 or over.

entries.old: Meat, dairy and most animal products may not be brought in from outside the EU; arrivals from within the EU face no routine customs limits for personal use.
entries.new: Revenue says that if you arrive from outside the EU with certain foodstuffs (mainly meat, milk, fish or products made from them), medicines, plants or animals, products of endangered species, or firearms, you must declare them to a customs officer.
entries.note: Restated as Revenue gives it (declare restricted foodstuffs); the claim about no customs limits within the EU was not checked and was removed.

entries.old: Arriving from the UK there are usually no routine passport checks (Common Travel Area), but airlines and ferries require photo ID and immigration officers can still carry out checks — non-Irish/non-British citizens should always carry their passport, and visa nationals need an Irish visa even when entering from the UK.
entries.new: British and Irish citizens travel freely between the UK and Ireland under the Common Travel Area. The UK government's travel advice says some airlines and ferry operators require a passport as identification, so check your carrier's rules; other nationalities should carry their passport, and visa-required nationals need an Irish visa even when entering from the UK.
entries.note: Restated per FCDO (carriers' passport requirement).

entries.old: Driving is on the LEFT, most rentals are manual (automatics cost more — book early), and rural roads on routes like the Ring of Kerry or Wild Atlantic Way are narrow with stone walls — take it slow and use pull-in passing spots.
entries.new: Traffic drives on the left in Ireland. Canada's travel advice says some roads can be uneven, narrow and winding, particularly in rural areas, and may become hazardous in severe weather.
entries.note: Restated per Canada; the manual-rental and stone-wall claims are unsupported.

entries.old: Expect four seasons in one day: pack waterproof layers year-round rather than an umbrella (Atlantic winds destroy them). Summer rarely exceeds 20°C and winter rarely drops far below freezing.
entries.new: (deleted)
entries.note: Temperature claims are not stated by any official source read; tip withdrawn.

entries.old: Yes. Ireland reintroduced the visa requirement for South African passport holders in June 2022, so the old visa-free access no longer applies. South Africans must obtain a short stay 'C' visa (€60 single entry) through the AVATS online system before traveling. Allow around 8 weeks.
entries.new: Yes. Ireland reintroduced the visa requirement for South African passport holders in June 2022, so the old visa-free access no longer applies. South Africans must obtain a short stay 'C' visa (€60 single entry) through the AVATS online system before traveling.
entries.note: Unsupported processing-time sentence ('around 8 weeks') deleted.

entries.old: Hebrew, Arabic, English (widely spoken)
entries.new: Hebrew, Arabic
entries.note: "English (widely spoken)" removed: not an official language. The Basic Law names Hebrew as the state language and gives Arabic a special status.

entries.new: False

entries.old: Historic city centers are restricted traffic zones (ZTL) — driving a rental car past the camera-enforced signs in Florence, Rome or Milan triggers automatic fines that follow you home.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says you need a pass to drive a private or hire car into the historic centre of many Italian cities. The boundaries are usually marked ZTL in black on a yellow background; cameras record registration numbers and drivers without a pass are fined.
entries.note: Rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Most cities charge a per-night tourist tax (typically €1–10 depending on city and hotel class, e.g. Up to €10 in Rome), usually paid at the accommodation and not included in booking prices.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says many major cities charge a small tourist tax, usually paid at your hotel and unlikely to be included in your booking. The rate varies by city and can depend on the hotel's star rating; hotels often ask for cash, so get a receipt.
entries.note: Rate figures are not stated by an official source; rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Validate regional train and bus tickets in the platform machines before boarding — traveling with an unvalidated ticket earns an on-the-spot fine.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says that if you buy a public transport ticket from a kiosk or machine, you must validate it before you start your journey: officials patrol and issue on-the-spot fines for unvalidated tickets. Some buses and trams accept contactless payment on board.
entries.note: Rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: General: 119; Police: 119; Ambulance: 110; Fire: 110
entries.new: Police: 119; Ambulance: 110; Fire: 110
entries.note: 119 is the police number, not a general one. The Jamaica Information Service quotes the Jamaica Fire Brigade: “110 is fire and ambulance emergencies”; the Government of Canada’s 911 for medical and fire is not used.

entries.old: Safe to drink

entries.old: Firearms and ammunition are prohibited without a permit obtained in advance — visitors have been arrested and jailed over a single forgotten round in hand luggage. | Cannabis is decriminalised in small amounts for personal use inside Jamaica, but carrying any across the border in either direction remains a criminal offense and airport screening catches it. | Camouflage-patterned clothing is restricted and can be confiscated from civilians. | Fresh produce, plants and meat products are controlled; declare anything agricultural on the C5 form.
entries.new: The Government of Canada says entering Jamaica with a firearm or even a single round of ammunition is considered a serious crime. | The UK FCDO says smoking marijuana (ganja) is illegal in Jamaica: possession of up to 2 ounces brings a J$500 fine, and severe penalties apply to other drug offences, including attempting to export narcotics. Departing visitors are thoroughly screened for drugs. | The UK FCDO says it is illegal to bring meat and dairy products into Jamaica, and the Government of Canada says fruits, vegetables, animals and animal products are strictly regulated.

entries.new: Japan Customs gives an adult duty-free allowance of 3 bottles of alcohol (about 760 ml each), 200 cigarettes, 2 ounces of perfume and other goods worth under ¥200,000 in total.

entries.old: Many common medications (e.g. Those containing pseudoephedrine or codeine above set limits) are restricted. Check import rules and obtain a Yunyu Kakunin-sho certificate where needed.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says some medications are banned in Japan, including Adderall, amphetamines, codeine, methamphetamines and pseudoephedrine, even with a prescription. Otherwise you may bring a one-month supply of prescription medicine or a two-month supply of non-prescription medicine, with a doctor's note.

entries.old: Cards are accepted in Amman hotels, malls and larger restaurants, but Petra-area shops, taxis and rural Jordan run on cash. Note that the dinar is a high-value currency (1 JOD is roughly 1.4 USD) — small notes are useful for tips and taxis.
entries.new: The UK Foreign Office says most places accept card payments but cash machines are widely available only in Amman and other major towns. Canada's travel advice says larger stores and restaurants in Amman and tourist areas accept credit cards, ATMs are limited outside the larger cities and Queen Alia airport, and only US dollars and euros are easily converted into dinars.
entries.note: Rewritten to what the FCDO and Canada state; the Petra/taxi cash claim and exchange rate had no official source.

entries.old: Spring (March–May) and fall (September–November) offer mild weather ideal for Petra, Wadi Rum and the Dead Sea; summers are very hot and winters can be surprisingly cold, with occasional snow in Amman.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Jordan. Canada's travel advice says the rainy season usually runs from November to March, with a risk of flash floods in wadis and on roads, and that snowfall is infrequent but can close roads.
entries.note: Withdrawn: the 'ideal for Petra' season claims had no official source.

entries.old: Kenya is a mobile-money country: M-Pesa dominates daily payments everywhere, from market stalls to taxis. Cards work in Nairobi and Mombasa hotels, malls and lodges; carry some shilling cash for small purchases and rural areas, or set up M-Pesa with a local SIM.
entries.new: The Government of Canada says credit cards are widely accepted in major cities and popular tourist destinations but not in remote locations, and that ATMs are widely available in cities. M-PESA mobile money is a common form of payment accepted across Kenya, including at national parks, which do not accept cash: they generally take credit cards, but at times only M-PESA works.
entries.note: "M-Pesa dominates daily payments everywhere, from market stalls to taxis" is not stated by any official source; text now follows the Government of Canada, which adds that national parks do not accept cash.

entries.old: July to October is the dry season and peak safari time — the Great Migration crosses the Maasai Mara roughly July to October. January to February is a second dry window, good for wildlife and the coast.
entries.new: No official source gives a best season. The Government of Canada says Kenya's two rainy seasons usually run from October to November and from March to mid-June, varying from year to year, and that seasonal flooding, flash floods and mudslides can hamper overland travel.
entries.note: Great Migration timing and "peak safari time" are not stated by any official source; the text now gives the rainy seasons the Government of Canada states.

entries.old: Plastic carrier bags are banned in Kenya — bringing one into the country (even a duty-free or zip-lock bag in your luggage) is an offense with heavy fines. Pack with cloth or paper bags.
entries.new: The Government of Canada says the use, manufacture or importation of plastic bags, including garbage and shopping bags, is illegal in Kenya; offenders, including tourists, can face fines of up to USD 40,000, up to two years in prison, or both.
entries.note: The duty-free / zip-lock bag detail is not stated by any official source read; replaced with the Government of Canada statement, including the penalties.

entries.old: Duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes and 1 liter of spirits per adult.
entries.new: The Kenya Revenue Authority's duty-free allowance: spirits (including liqueurs) or wine up to 1 liter, or wine up to 2 liters; perfume and toilet water up to half a liter, of which no more than a quarter may be perfume; and cigarettes, cigars, cheroots, cigarillos, tobacco and snuff up to 250 g in all.
entries.note: KRA sets the tobacco allowance by weight (250 g of all tobacco products), not as 200 cigarettes, and allows 2 liters if the drink is wine; perfume allowance added.

entries.old: …the Maasai Mara is around 100–200 USD per adult per day in high season…
entries.new: According to the Government of Canada, national parks do not accept cash: they generally take credit cards, but at times, because of technical problems, only M-PESA mobile money works. Check whether park fees are included in your safari price.
entries.note: Park fee amounts are not stated by any official source read and were removed.

entries.old: July to October, during the dry season, when the Great Migration is in the Maasai Mara…
entries.new: No official source gives a best safari season. The Government of Canada says Kenya's two rainy seasons usually run from October to November and from March to mid-June, varying from year to year, and that seasonal flooding can hamper overland travel. Budget for park fees, which are often charged on top of a safari price; parks do not accept cash.
entries.note: Migration timing and best-season claims are not stated by any official source; answer now gives the official rainy seasons.

entries.old: Kiribati runs on cash. Card acceptance is close to non-existent outside one or two hotels on South Tarawa, ATMs are few and can be empty or offline, and there is no reliable way to draw money on the outer islands. Bring enough Australian dollars in cash for the whole trip, in small denominations.
entries.new: The UK government says very few places in Kiribati accept credit cards, and that there are ATMs at Bank of Kiribati and ANZ branches in Betio, Bairiki and Bikenibeu on Tarawa. Canada's travel advice says the number of ATMs is limited.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: May to October is the drier, slightly less humid half of the year on Tarawa and the best window for bonefishing and diving. Kiribati sits on the equator outside the main cyclone belt, so heat and rainfall — not storms — decide the season.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season in the South Pacific runs from November to April, when severe rainstorms can disrupt travel and essential services.
entries.note: Replaced with the climate statement the cited source supports.

entries.old: Kiribati is an atoll nation with strict quarantine rules: fresh food, seeds, plants and soil-covered equipment must be declared and may be refused entry. | Alcohol imports are limited and licensing is restricted on some islands. Check local rules before bringing bottles as gifts. | The Phoenix Islands Protected Area and several outer islands need permission from the relevant ministry before you may visit or land; arrange it well in advance through the Immigration Division or your tour operator.
entries.new: The UK government says there is a strict quarantine regime for importing food, plant and animal (including fish) products. | Canada's travel advice says importing firearms, ammunition, explosives, counterfeit money and goods, knives and pornography is strictly prohibited.
entries.note: Only what an official source states is kept, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: Treat Kiribati as a cash-only country. Bring Australian dollars for the entire stay including the departure taxes and any boat charter. A card that fails on South Tarawa cannot be rescued, and there is no banking at all on most outer islands.
entries.new: Bring enough cash for the whole stay. The UK government says very few places accept credit cards and that ATMs are found only at bank branches in Betio, Bairiki and Bikenibeu on Tarawa.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Medical facilities are very limited. Tungaru Central Hospital handles basic emergencies; anything beyond that requires evacuation to Fiji or Australia, which depends on flight availability. Carry a full personal medical kit and any prescription drugs you need, plus a copy of the prescription.
entries.new: The UK government says medical facilities at the general hospital in Tarawa are modest and that any non-basic treatment usually means medical evacuation. Carry your own medicines with a copy of the prescription, and insurance that covers evacuation by air ambulance.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Tarawa is served by only a few international flights a week, mainly from Nadi and Brisbane via Nauru, and cancellations cascade. Leave two or three buffer days before any onward international connection, and never book a same-day connection out of Fiji.
entries.new: International flights are few, so leave buffer days before any onward international connection.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Kiribati spans three time zones across 3,000 km — Tarawa and the Gilberts are UTC+12, the Phoenix Islands UTC+13 and the Line Islands, including Kiritimati, UTC+14, the earliest time zone on earth. Check which group your flight lands in before you calculate a connection.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports it.

entries.old: Do not drink tap or well water. Use bottled, boiled or treated water, including for brushing teeth. Equatorial sun on a treeless atoll is fierce even on cloudy days, so plan for shade, high-factor sunscreen and far more water than you think you need.
entries.new: Equatorial sun on an atoll is fierce even on cloudy days, so plan for shade, high-factor sunscreen and plenty of drinking water.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Your entry permission covers the country, but travel to the outer islands is limited by transport rather than paperwork, and the Phoenix Islands Protected Area needs a permit from the responsible ministry. Kiritimati (Christmas Island) in the Line Islands has its own international flights and its own time zone. Plan it as a separate leg from Tarawa, not a day trip.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports it.

entries.old: Barely. A couple of hotels on South Tarawa take cards, ATMs are scarce and unreliable, and the outer islands have no banking. Kiribati uses the Australian dollar, so bring cash in AUD and budget for the whole trip in advance.
entries.new: Barely. The UK government says very few places accept credit cards, and ATMs are found at Bank of Kiribati and ANZ branches in Betio, Bairiki and Bikenibeu on Tarawa. Kiribati uses the Australian dollar, so bring cash in AUD and budget for the whole trip in advance.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.
