entries.old: Kosovo uses the euro even though it is not in the eurozone. Cards work in Pristina and Prizren hotels, supermarkets and bigger restaurants, but much of daily life runs on cash. Carry euros in small denominations, especially outside the cities.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Kosovo's economy is largely cash-based, with credit cards accepted in some larger establishments and cash machines in urban centres. Australia's Smartraveller adds that road tolls and fines must be paid in cash.
entries.note: Rewritten to Canada's advice; card acceptance lowered from 'widely in cities' to 'limited'.

entries.old: May–September is warm and lively, ideal for Pristina’s café scene, Prizren’s old town and hiking in the Rugova and Sharr mountains; winters are cold but bring cheap skiing at Brezovica.
entries.new: No official source we checked gives seasonal guidance for Kosovo; the months shown are not an official recommendation. Canada's travel advice says forest fires are common between June and September, and heavy rains in spring and summer can cause flooding and landslides.
entries.note: The café, hiking and Brezovica skiing claims had no official source.

entries.old: Standard duty-free allowances apply for tobacco and alcohol — roughly 200 cigarettes and 1 liter of spirits per adult; confirm current limits with Kosovo Customs. | Vehicles need valid insurance recognized in Kosovo. Many European Green Cards exclude Kosovo, and border insurance must then be bought on arrival.
entries.new: Kosovo Customs allows each traveller aged 17 or over to bring in duty-free 200 cigarettes (or 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 50 g of tobacco), 1 litre of spirits over 22% (or 1 litre of weaker spirits or sparkling wine) and 2 litres of still wine. | The UK government says European Green Card vehicle insurance is not valid in Kosovo: buy local third-party insurance at the border or in the nearest town, and carry enough euros in cash to pay for it.
entries.note: Allowances confirmed and completed from Kosovo Customs; the UK says Green Cards are not valid at all, not that 'many' exclude Kosovo.

entries.old: Serbia treats direct arrival into Kosovo as an illegal entry into its territory: if you plan to continue from Kosovo into Serbia, enter Serbia first (or route via a third country) — travelers with only a Kosovo entry stamp are routinely refused at Serbian crossings.
entries.new: The UK government says you cannot travel from Kosovo to Serbia without a Serbian entry stamp and are likely to be refused entry without one; Serbia does not treat its crossing points with Kosovo as international border crossings. If you plan to continue to Serbia, enter Serbia first or route through a third country.
entries.note: Attributed to the UK government.

entries.old: The Serb-majority northern municipalities around Mitrovica see periodic unrest. Check current advice before visiting the north and stay away from demonstrations and roadblocks.
entries.new: Canada advises against non-essential travel to northern Kosovo, and the UK government warns that protests in Zvečan, Zubin Potok, Leposavić and north Mitrovica have at times turned violent. Check current advice before visiting the north and avoid demonstrations.
entries.note: Attributed to the Canadian and UK advice.

entries.old: Driving in? Check whether your Green Card insurance actually covers Kosovo. Many policies exclude it, and you must then buy local border insurance on arrival; keep the receipt for checkpoints.
entries.new: Driving in? The UK government says European Green Card insurance is not valid in Kosovo, so buy local third-party insurance at the border or in the nearest town and carry euros in cash to pay for it.
entries.note: The UK says Green Cards are not valid at all, not that 'many policies' exclude Kosovo.

entries.old: Kosovo runs on euro cash outside the big cities. Keep small notes handy for taxis, bakeries and mountain guesthouses, and expect some places to struggle to change €50 notes.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Kosovo's economy is largely cash-based and cards are accepted only in some larger establishments, and Australia's Smartraveller says road tolls and fines must be paid in cash. Keep euros on you.
entries.note: The claim that places struggle to change €50 notes had no source.

entries.old: Crossings operate, but direction matters: Serbia does not recognize Kosovo’s international border points, so if you entered Kosovo directly (by air or from Albania, North Macedonia or Montenegro), Serbia may refuse you entry as having entered Serbia illegally. Visit Serbia first, or route through a third country.
entries.new: Crossings operate, but direction matters. The UK government says Serbia does not consider its crossing points with Kosovo to be official international border crossings: you can travel from Serbia to Kosovo and back, but not from Kosovo into Serbia without a Serbian entry stamp. If you entered Kosovo directly, route through a third country.
entries.note: Attributed to the UK government.

entries.old: The euro is Kosovo’s official currency, even though Kosovo is not an EU or eurozone member. Cards are fine in city hotels and supermarkets, but carry euro cash in small denominations for everything else; in a few Serb-majority areas the Serbian dinar also circulates unofficially.
entries.new: The euro. Canada's travel advice says Kosovo's economy is largely cash-based, with credit cards accepted in some larger establishments and cash machines in urban centres, so carry euro cash.
entries.note: The claim that the Serbian dinar circulates unofficially had no source.

entries.old: No — Kosovo is outside the EU and Schengen, so days spent there do not count against your Schengen 90/180-day allowance. That makes Kosovo (like its Balkan neighbors) a popular stop for travelers resetting their Schengen clock.
entries.new: No — Kosovo is outside the EU and the Schengen Area, so days spent there do not count against your Schengen 90/180-day allowance.
entries.note: Removed the unsupported claim that Kosovo is a popular stop for resetting the Schengen clock.

entries.old: true
entries.new: false
entries.note: No official source we could read states that Kuwait's tap water is safe to drink (only press reports of ministry statements); withdrawn under the unconfirmed-is-not-published rule.

entries.old: Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere in Kuwait City, from malls to taxis. Cash is rarely needed beyond small souq purchases and tips.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says credit cards and US dollars are widely accepted and ATMs are available nationwide, but that taxi drivers usually accept payment only in cash.
entries.note: Enums confirmed. Text rewritten to Canada's advice; the claim that taxis take cards contradicts Canada (taxis usually cash only).

entries.old: November to March brings mild, pleasant weather for the Corniche, souqs and desert trips; summer is among the hottest on Earth, regularly exceeding 45°C.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Kuwait faces extreme heat, especially from June to August, with temperatures well above 40°C and high humidity; sand and dust storms may occur between May and August, and the rainy season, with occasional heavy rain and flooding, runs from November to April.
entries.note: 'Regularly exceeding 45°C' is not stated; climate restated per Canada.

entries.old: Alcohol may not be brought into Kuwait in any quantity, including duty-free purchases made en route. The country is completely dry.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says it is illegal to import narcotics, alcohol, gambling machines, pork and pork products, or pornographic material into Kuwait; Canada's travel advice says alcohol cannot be legally purchased or imported, and that possessing or consuming it is illegal.
entries.note: Restated per FCDO and Canada; the duty-free remark is not stated.

entries.old: Narcotics, pork products and pornographic material are prohibited; medications containing controlled substances need a prescription.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says all visitors must obtain permission from the Kuwaiti authorities before arrival to carry certain prescription drugs, including many commonly prescribed medications.
entries.note: Restated per FCDO: prior permission is needed for certain prescription medicines, not just a prescription.

entries.old: Kuwait is a fully dry country — alcohol is illegal to import, buy or consume anywhere, with penalties including fines, imprisonment and deportation.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says alcohol is illegal in Kuwait: buying, selling or carrying it, as well as public intoxication, can lead to fines, imprisonment and deportation.
entries.note: Restated per FCDO.

entries.old: Travelers whose passports show Israeli stamps or visas are routinely refused entry to Kuwait — travel on a clean passport if you have previously visited Israel.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says that if your passport contains an Israeli stamp, you may be refused a visa or entry to Kuwait; Canada's travel advice reports Canadians being denied entry because of Israeli visas or stamps, or Egyptian or Jordanian border stamps from crossings with Israel.
entries.note: 'Routinely refused' overstated; restated per FCDO and Canada.

entries.old: From June to September temperatures regularly exceed 45°C. Plan outdoor activities for early morning or after dark and stay hydrated.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Kuwait faces extreme heat, especially from June to August, with temperatures well above 40°C and high humidity, and that the symptoms of dehydration and heatstroke, which can both be fatal, are worth knowing.
entries.note: 'Regularly exceed 45°C' is not stated; restated per Canada.

entries.old: During Ramadan, eating, drinking or smoking in public during daylight hours is an offense for everyone, including visitors — hotels serve food discreetly.
entries.new: The UK government's travel advice says that during Ramadan you should not eat, drink, smoke or chew gum in public in the daytime, including in your car, and that hotels and restaurants serving food in fasting hours may screen you from Muslim guests.
entries.note: That it is 'an offense for everyone' is not stated; restated as the FCDO's advice.

entries.old: Apply for the eVisa only through the Kuwait Ministry of Interior's official portal — third-party websites charge large markups for the same visa.
entries.new: Apply for the eVisa only through the Kuwait Ministry of Interior's official Kuwait Visa platform (kuwaitvisa.moi.gov.kw).
entries.note: Unsupported claim about third-party markups deleted.

entries.old: Eligible nationalities pay KWD 3 at Kuwait International Airport for a tourist visa on arrival, typically allowing a stay of up to three months. Applying online in advance through the official eVisa portal is faster and avoids lines at the visa counter.
entries.new: Eligible nationalities pay KWD 3 at Kuwait International Airport for a tourist visa on arrival, typically allowing a stay of up to three months. Canada's travel advice recommends applying for the eVisa before arrival to avoid delays or complications on entry.
entries.note: 'Faster and avoids lines' replaced with Canada's stated reason.

entries.old: The tourist eVisa costs KWD 3 (roughly USD 10). Apply only through the Ministry of Interior's official portal and confirm the exact fee during the application — third-party sites add heavy service charges.
entries.new: The tourist eVisa costs KWD 3 (roughly USD 10). Apply only through the Ministry of Interior's official portal and confirm the exact fee during the application.
entries.note: Unsupported claim about third-party service charges deleted.

entries.old: No. Kuwait does not admit Israeli passport holders, and travelers of any nationality whose passports show Israeli stamps or visas are routinely refused entry. Use a clean passport if you have previously visited Israel.
entries.new: No. Kuwait does not admit Israeli passport holders. The UK government's travel advice says travellers whose passports contain an Israeli stamp may be refused a visa or entry, and Canada's travel advice reports Canadians being denied entry because of Israeli visas or stamps, or Egyptian or Jordanian border stamps from crossings with Israel.
entries.note: 'Routinely refused' overstated; restated per FCDO and Canada.

entries.old: No. Kuwait is completely dry — alcohol cannot legally be imported, sold or consumed anywhere in the country, including hotels, and penalties for violations are severe.
entries.new: No. Canada's travel advice says possession and consumption of alcohol are illegal in Kuwait and that alcohol cannot be legally purchased or imported; penalties include heavy fines, imprisonment or deportation.
entries.note: Restated per Canada.

entries.old: The US dollar circulates alongside the Liberian dollar and is accepted everywhere. Bring US dollars in cash. Cards work only at a handful of Monrovia hotels, and ATMs dispensing US dollars are scarce.

A few ATMs in Monrovia accept Visa cards, but they often run out of money; it advises bringing enough US dollars to cover all expenses.

entries.old: November to April is the dry season and the practical window for travel — Monrovia is one of the world's wettest capitals, and the May–October rains flood roads across the country.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season runs from May to November, when heavy rain can cause flash flooding and make roads impassable, and that the dry season from December to March brings the harmattan, a dusty wind that can severely limit visibility.

entries.old: Bring clean, recent US dollar notes. They are legal tender alongside the Liberian dollar and by far the most practical way to pay; torn or pre-2009 bills are often refused.
entries.new: Bring US dollars in cash. The UK Foreign Office advises bringing enough to cover all expenses: Liberia is predominantly cash-based, cards are not generally accepted, and banks can run short of both US and Liberian dollars.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: From May to October Liberia gets some of the heaviest rainfall on earth — up-country roads become impassable and flights are disrupted, so plan travel for the November–April dry season.
entries.new: Canada and the UK both say the rainy season runs from May to November, when many roads become impassable — plan up-country travel for the dry months.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: Liberia uses US-style 120 V sockets (types A and B) — unusual for Africa — and mains power is unreliable, so pack a power bank and check chargers for dual voltage.

entries.old: US dollars in cash. The US dollar is used alongside the Liberian dollar for everyday payments, cards are accepted almost nowhere, and ATMs are unreliable. Bring enough clean, recent US notes for your whole stay.
entries.new: US dollars in cash. The UK Foreign Office says Liberia remains predominantly cash-based, cards are not generally accepted except at a few major hotels and some larger supermarkets, and ATMs often run out of money; it advises bringing enough US dollars to cover all expenses.

Canada says Lithuania enforces an EU entry ban on vehicles with Russian or Belarusian plates, with exceptions. Rules change at short notice.

The UK government says only one crossing point remains open, Medininkai–Kamenny Log, and only by private vehicle — scheduled buses are not running — and Lithuania denies entry to Belarus-registered cars, with some exemptions. Check the current rules before attempting an overland trip.

entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the military took over on 14 October 2025 after large-scale demonstrations and announced a two-year transition. Demonstrations are frequent and can turn violent: avoid them and large gatherings, and follow local news.

entries.old: Road travel is slow — a few hundred kilometers can take a full day on degraded roads — so most visitors use domestic flights to cover long distances.

entries.old: Malaria is present year-round in coastal and lowland areas. Take prophylaxis, use repellent and sleep under nets; the central highlands carry lower risk.

entries.note: Regional risk claims removed; rewritten to Canadian travel advice.

entries.old: Most trips are trouble-free, but take petty and opportunistic crime seriously in Antananarivo and on isolated beaches, avoid demonstrations given the unsettled political situation, and plan around the November–April cyclone season. Check your government's travel advice before booking.

Canada's travel advice says petty crime is common throughout the country, that violent crime is reported in all regions, and that armed gangs have assaulted tourists in isolated areas such as beaches and national parks. Demonstrations are frequent and can turn violent, and the UK FCDO says the cyclone season normally runs from November to April.

Declare anything organic, including fruit picked up on the island-hopper. | Firearms and ammunition are prohibited without prior authorization, and are taken seriously at Majuro's small airport. | Visiting Bikini, Enewetak, Rongelap and other atolls affected by the US nuclear testing program requires permission from the local atoll council or the national government — arrange it long before you arrive. | Kwajalein island hosts a US Army garrison and is not open to casual visitors: access needs US military sponsorship, separate from your RMI entry permission. Neighboring Ebeye is not restricted in the same way.
entries.new: The UK government says it is illegal to import firearms, ammunition and drugs.
entries.note: Only what an official source states is kept, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: Medical care is basic. Majuro Hospital handles routine emergencies, Ebeye has a clinic, and the outer atolls have health assistants only. Anything serious means a flight to Honolulu or Guam. Carry your own medications with prescriptions, and insurance that names medical evacuation.
entries.new: The UK government says medical facilities are very limited. Bring enough prescription medicine for your stay, and insurance that covers all medical costs including medical evacuation.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Majuro is reached mainly by the United island-hopper between Honolulu and Guam and by Nauru Airlines from Brisbane, each running only a few times a week. A missed or canceled flight can cost you several days, so leave buffer time and never book a tight onward international connection.
entries.new: International flights are few, so leave buffer time and avoid tight onward international connections.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Bikini, Enewetak, Rongelap and other atolls affected by the nuclear testing program are not casual destinations — visits need permission from the atoll council or the national government, and Bikini diving depends on a charter operating that season. Kwajalein island requires US military sponsorship, though Ebeye does not.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports it.

entries.old: Do not drink the tap water. Most supply is rainwater catchment and droughts strain it. Stick to bottled or boiled water, and bring small-denomination US dollars, since ATMs are limited to Majuro and Ebeye and can be empty.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller advises drinking boiled or bottled water, and says there are only a few ATMs, none of them at the airport, and that the departure fee must be paid in US dollars cash.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Only with permission. Bikini, Enewetak and Rongelap are governed by their atoll councils and the national government, and access depends on an authorized charter or liveaboard operating that season. Do not plan on turning up in Majuro and arranging it there. The approvals and the boat both need months of notice.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports it.

entries.old: No, it is not an entry requirement and nobody checks it. Given how far Majuro is from a full hospital, insurance that explicitly covers medical evacuation is the single most valuable thing to arrange before you fly, especially if you intend to dive.
entries.new: No official source we could read makes travel insurance a condition of entry. The UK government advises comprehensive insurance covering all medical costs, including medical evacuation, because medical facilities are very limited.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Cards work only at a handful of Nouakchott hotels and supermarkets. This is a cash economy. Change euros or dollars at banks or licensed bureaux; locals often still quote prices in pre-2018 "old" ouguiya (ten times the current unit), so confirm which is meant.
entries.new: The UK government says Mauritania is mainly a cash-based society: a few hotels in Nouakchott and Nouadhibou accept credit cards (some only Visa), and some ATMs accept foreign cards. US dollars and euros can be exchanged at banks, some hotels and official bureaux de change. Canada and Australia add that you must declare foreign currency on arrival and cannot leave with more than you declared.
entries.note: Rewritten to the UK, Canadian and Australian advice; the 'old ouguiya' pricing claim had no source.

entries.old: November to March is the cool season — the only comfortable window for the Sahara, the Adrar oases and the iron-ore train; from April the interior becomes dangerously hot.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season runs from July to October, when seasonal flooding can make roads impassable. No official source names a best season.
entries.note: The Sahara, Adrar and iron-ore-train claims had no official source.

entries.old: Alcohol may not be brought into Mauritania. It is a dry country and importing it is prohibited. | Drones and professional camera equipment can attract questions at the border. Carry paperwork for anything valuable.
entries.new: The UK government says it is illegal for Muslims and non-Muslims alike to import or consume alcohol or pork products. Baggage is scanned on arrival at Nouakchott airport and vehicles may be searched at land borders; alcohol and pork are confiscated, and people carrying them can be arrested or fined.
entries.note: Rewritten to the UK advice; the drone and camera-equipment note had no source.

entries.old: Stay out of the areas near the Mali border and the far east. They are under do-not-travel advisories. Stick to the west-coast corridor and the Adrar, ideally with a local operator.
entries.new: The UK government advises against all travel to areas within 25 km of the Malian border in the south, including Khabou, and to the east of a line through Kankossa, Akhreijit, Ghallaouia, Zouérat and Fdérik; Canada advises against all travel to northern and eastern Mauritania. Check current advice before planning any route.
entries.note: Aligned with the areas the UK and Canada name.

entries.old: Bring the eVisa fee in exact cash — euros or US dollars. Cards are not accepted at the airport counters and change is rarely given.
entries.new: The UK government says the e-visa fee is paid on arrival in exact cash in euros or US dollars, and that change and receipts are not given. Print a copy of your e-visa to show on arrival.
entries.note: Attributed to the UK government.

entries.old: Police checkpoints are frequent on every intercity road. Carry a stack of printed passport copies ("fiches") listing your details and route to hand over — it saves long stops.
entries.new: The UK government advises always carrying copies of your photo ID, especially outside Nouakchott, where there are police checkpoints.
entries.note: The 'fiches' listing your route had no official source.

entries.old: Mauritania is a dry country — alcohol may not be imported or consumed, including anything bought in duty-free en route.
entries.new: The UK government says it is illegal for anyone, Muslim or not, to import or consume alcohol in Mauritania, and Australia's Smartraveller says transporting any alcohol is also illegal unless authorised.
entries.note: Attributed to the UK and Australian advice.

entries.old: The Nouadhibou–Zouérat iron-ore train can be ridden by travelers, but conditions in the open ore wagons are harsh. Bring goggles, warm layers for the night and water, or book the single passenger carriage.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports this tip.

entries.old: The traveled west of the country — Nouakchott, Nouadhibou, the Banc d'Arguin coast and the Adrar — has a growing tourist circuit and is generally calm, but border areas with Mali and the remote east are high-risk and under do-not-travel advisories. Check current advisories and use a local operator for desert itineraries.
entries.new: The UK government advises against all travel to areas within 25 km of the Malian border and to the east of the country, and Canada advises against all travel to northern and eastern Mauritania, citing extremist groups, armed smugglers and a high risk of kidnapping, with Westerners a preferred target. Check current advisories before planning a trip.
entries.note: The claims about a 'growing tourist circuit' and a 'generally calm' west had no source.

entries.old: Rarely — outside a few Nouakchott hotels it is cash only. Bring euros or US dollars to exchange, and note that prices are sometimes quoted in "old" ouguiya worth a tenth of the current MRU unit.
entries.new: Rarely. The UK government says Mauritania is mainly a cash-based society, with only a few hotels in Nouakchott and Nouadhibou accepting credit cards and some ATMs taking foreign cards. Bring US dollars or euros to exchange at banks or official bureaux de change, and declare foreign currency on arrival.
entries.note: The 'old ouguiya' pricing claim had no source.

entries.old: The FSM is four states — Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae — spread over 2,700 km. Each has its own airport, customs of its own, and often only a few flights a week; plan island-hopping around the United Airlines "island hopper" schedule.

entries.old: Thighs are considered far more revealing than shoulders in much of Micronesia — swimwear is for the water, and a sarong or long shorts is the respectful choice in villages and towns.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says to dress conservatively, behave discreetly and respect religious and social traditions. It also says drunkenness and drinking in public places are punishable offences.

entries.old: How do you actually get to Micronesia? — Almost everyone arrives on the United "island hopper" service that links Guam and Honolulu via Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae and Kwajalein, or on the Guam–Yap flights. Seats are limited and the schedule is thin, so book flights before locking in hotels.

entries.old: Your accommodation must register you with the local tourist board within 24 hours — hotels do it automatically, but private hosts sometimes forget; ask for the registration slip and keep it until you leave.

entries.old: Montenegro uses the euro even though it is not an EU member. No currency exchange needed if you arrive from the eurozone, but bring cash for small places.
entries.new: Montenegro uses the euro although it is not an EU member: the European Central Bank lists it among the countries that use the euro without a formal arrangement. No currency exchange is needed if you arrive from the euro area.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources say, attributed.

entries.old: Cards are accepted in Maputo hotels, supermarkets and the bigger beach lodges; everywhere else cash rules. US dollars and South African rand are widely taken in tourist areas, but carry small metical notes up-country.

entries.old: May to October is the dry, cooler season — ideal for beaches, diving and safaris. November to April is hot and humid, with cyclone risk along the coast roughly January to March.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy and hot season runs from November to April, when cyclones occur mainly along the coast and seasonal flooding can make roads impassable.
entries.note: Replaced with the climate statement the cited source supports.

entries.old: Drones require prior authorization from the civil aviation authority — undeclared drones are regularly confiscated at entry.

entries.old: Avoid Cabo Delgado province in the far north, where an insurgency continues, including Pemba's surroundings when advisories say so. The main beach destinations from Maputo up to Vilankulo are far from the affected area.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller says do not travel to Cabo Delgado province, the Erati and Memba districts of Nampula province, or the Marrupa and Mecula districts of Niassa province, because of terrorism, violent crime and kidnapping.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Carry your passport with entry stamp (or a notarised copy) at all times — police checkpoints are frequent and fines for missing documents are common.
entries.new: Carry your passport at all times. The UK government says police patrols and checkpoints are common and will not accept copies or photos of it.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Cyclone and heavy-rain season runs roughly December to March, especially along the central and northern coast — roads flood and ferries stop. Check forecasts if traveling in that window.
entries.new: The UK government says cyclones and floods are common in the rainy season from November to April, often causing landslides, road closures and disruption to transport. Check forecasts if travelling then.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: The main beach circuit in the south and center is generally fine with normal precautions. The serious security problem is confined to Cabo Delgado province in the far north. Check current advisories, carry your documents, and avoid driving at night.
entries.new: Check current advisories before you go. Australia's Smartraveller advises a high degree of caution in Mozambique overall and says do not travel to Cabo Delgado province and parts of Nampula and Niassa provinces, nor on stretches of the EN1 and EN6 roads. The UK government says you must carry your passport at all times.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Myanmar runs on cash. International cards work only at a handful of top hotels, ATMs are unreliable and often empty, and the exchange rate situation is volatile. Bring pristine US dollar notes to change into kyat.
entries.new: The UK government says Myanmar is largely a cash-based society: many ATMs do not accept international cards, many shops take only cash, and you should phone ahead if you want to pay a hotel or restaurant by card. Canada says US dollars are widely accepted but only as new, unmarked, undamaged notes, and that changing money anywhere other than an authorised exchange is illegal.
entries.note: Rewritten to the UK and Canadian advice.
Canada puts November in the May–November monsoon.

entries.old: November to February is the cool, dry season — the best weather for Bagan and Mandalay. March to May is extremely hot, and the monsoon runs roughly June to October.
entries.new: The UK government gives the rainy season as May to October; Canada gives May to November and says cyclones usually occur between April and October. No official source names a best season; the months shown fall outside both.
entries.note: The Bagan/Mandalay recommendation had no official source.

entries.old: Most governments advise against all nonessential travel to Myanmar, and against all travel to large parts of the country. Fighting can erupt with little warning, martial-law areas are off-limits, and consular help on the ground is very limited.
entries.new: Canada strongly advises against all travel to Myanmar and Australia says do not travel; the UK advises against all travel to much of the country, including Rakhine, Kachin, Chin and Shan North, and against all but essential travel to Mandalay Region. Canada reports regime airstrikes and drone strikes, and says embassy staff need government permission to travel outside Yangon.
entries.note: Attributed and aligned with what the three governments advise; martial-law claims had no source.

entries.old: Land crossings with Thailand, China and India are largely closed or barred to foreigners. Do not plan an overland entry or exit elsewhere.
entries.new: Canada advises against all travel to Myanmar, including through its land borders, and says crossings may close with little or no notice or be restricted to nationals of the neighbouring state. The eVisa is valid only for arrival at Yangon, Mandalay and Nay Pyi Taw international airports and the Kawthaung land checkpoint.

entries.old: Bring enough pristine, unfolded US dollar bills for your whole trip — torn or marked notes are refused, international cards rarely work, and ATMs cannot be relied on.
entries.new: Bring enough US dollars for your stay: the UK government says Myanmar is largely cash-based and many ATMs do not accept international cards, and that notes must be in good condition, without pen marks, folds or tears. Exchange counters may refuse notes whose serial numbers start AB or CB.

entries.old: Power cuts and internet or mobile-data shutdowns are frequent. Download offline maps, keep some cash and your documents accessible, and note your embassy's contact details on paper.
entries.new: The UK government says the authorities control internet access and periodically cut it off entirely, and that some services, including Facebook and WhatsApp, are blocked. Canada advises charging your phone and carrying power banks in case of internet, communication and power outages.
entries.note: Attributed to the UK and Canadian advice.

entries.old: Shoes and socks come off at every pagoda and monastery, including the long walkways at Shwedagon. Dress with shoulders and knees covered, and step around, never over, seated monks.
entries.new: The UK government says to remove shoes and socks before entering a pagoda or monastery, and that shorts, short skirts and sleeveless tops can cause offence at religious sites.

entries.new: Register with the police soon after you arrive: Canada says within 24 hours, the UK government within 48 hours. Hotels and other commercial accommodation register you at check-in; otherwise register at the nearest police station and keep the document until you leave.
entries.note: Canada gives 24 hours, the UK 48; the tip now names both.

entries.old: Pay in denars (MKD). Cards work in cities, but taxis, markets and villages want cash, and prices quoted in euros usually build in a bad exchange rate.
entries.new: Carry denars in cash: Canada says the economy is mostly cash-based and cards are accepted only in some larger establishments. Change money only at banks or official exchanges, not with street dealers (UK government).
entries.note: The claim that euro prices build in a bad exchange rate had no source.

entries.old: Lake Ohrid is the summer highlight — July and August are busiest; June and September still have warm water, cheaper rooms and far fewer crowds.

entries.old: Skopje suffers some of Europe's worst winter air pollution (roughly November–February) — travelers with respiratory conditions should check air-quality forecasts and plan accordingly.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says smoke haze and air pollution can be extremely hazardous, usually worst in winter because of coal and wood heating, and Australia's Smartraveller names Skopje. Travellers with breathing conditions should check air-quality levels.
entries.note: Attributed to the Canadian and Australian advice.

entries.old: The Macedonian denar (MKD). Cards are fine in cities, but carry denar cash for taxis, bazaars and the countryside — euros are sometimes accepted informally at poor rates.
entries.new: The Macedonian denar (MKD). Canada's travel advice says the economy is mostly cash-based, with credit cards accepted in some larger establishments and ATMs in urban centres, so carry denar cash. Australia's Smartraveller says the denar cannot be changed outside North Macedonia.
entries.note: The claim that euros are accepted informally at poor rates had no source.

entries.old: May–September brings long days, open mountain roads and the midnight sun in the north; for northern lights aim for September–March in Tromsø or Lofoten instead.

entries.old: Dress conservatively — long trousers and covered shoulders; a headscarf is useful for women visiting mosques. During Ramadan, avoid eating, drinking or smoking in public in daylight hours.
entries.new: The UK FCDO advises men and women to cover their shoulders and legs in public, and women to cover their heads in mosques, holy places and rural areas. During Ramadan it advises not eating, drinking or smoking in public in the daytime.
entries.note: Rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: It depends heavily on where you go. The northern mountain areas and the main cities host growing numbers of tourists without incident, but several governments advise against travel to border regions, parts of Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Read your government's current advisory, register your trip and consider traveling with a reputable local operator.
entries.new: It depends heavily on where you go. The UK FCDO advises against all travel within 10 miles of the Afghan border and to Balochistan and parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and against all but essential travel to Azad Jammu and Kashmir. Read your government's current advice before you book.
entries.note: Unsupported claim about tourist numbers removed; rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Reef-toxic sunscreen is banned — products containing oxybenzone, octinoxate and several related chemicals are confiscated at the airport and can carry a fine. Bring mineral (zinc oxide) sunscreen instead. | Taking sea turtles, giant clams, coral or other protected marine life or souvenirs made from them is illegal. | Biosecurity is strict on fresh produce, seeds, plants and animal products.
entries.new: It is illegal to bring reef-toxic sunscreen into Palau: the UK FCDO says customs will confiscate any found in your baggage, and permitted sunscreens generally have zinc oxide or titanium dioxide as the active ingredient. | Declare personal items worth more than US$400, and anything that may be prohibited or dutiable, on the Palau entry form (UK FCDO).

entries.new: No official source we could read describes card acceptance in Panama. Canada's travel advice says the balboa is used interchangeably with the US dollar, and that because of counterfeit US$50 and US$100 bills you should carry only small US notes.

entries.note: Months narrowed to January–March, outside the April–December rainy season Canada states; the dry-season and price claims had no official source.

Dive resorts, Milne Bay, Tufi and the Sepik are generally calmer.

entries.old: Cards are widely accepted in Lima, Cusco and Arequipa hotels, restaurants and shops, but cash rules in markets, small towns, taxis and the countryside. Carry soles in small notes — change for 100-sol bills is scarce — and use ATMs inside banks or malls.

entries.old: May to September is the dry season in the Andes — the best window for Cusco, Machu Picchu and trekking (book the Inca Trail months ahead); Lima's coast is gray then but pleasant December–March.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season in the Peruvian Andes runs from November to May, when flooding and landslides can close tourist areas, and that forest fires are common in the dry season from June to October.
entries.note: Replaced with the climate statement the cited source supports.

entries.old: There is no paper entry form. The old Andean Migration Card (TAM) is digital and generated automatically at passport control; note the number of days written or stamped, as that is your permitted stay. | Personal electronics such as a laptop and phone enter duty-free; strict rules protect archaeological artefacts — exporting antiques or pre-Columbian items is a crime. | Coca leaves and coca tea are legal in Peru but illegal to take into most other countries, including the US and the EU.
entries.new: There is no paper entry form. The old Andean Migration Card (TAM) is digital and generated automatically at passport control; note the number of days written or stamped, as that is your permitted stay. | The UK government says it is illegal to remove any archaeological artefacts from Peru without authorisation. | The UK government advises against taking coca leaves or coca tea out of Peru, as importing them into the UK is illegal; check the rules of your next destination.
entries.note: Only what an official source states is kept, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: Cusco sits at 3,400 m. Plan a light first day, hydrate, and consider acclimatising in the lower Sacred Valley (2,800 m) before the city or any trek. Altitude sickness can hit anyone regardless of fitness.
entries.new: The UK government says altitude sickness is a serious risk in parts of Peru, including Cusco, Puno, the Colca Canyon and Kuelap. Plan a light first day, stay hydrated and learn the symptoms.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Machu Picchu entry tickets are limited, timed and sold out weeks ahead in high season (June–August). Buy them and Inca Trail permits well in advance through official channels only.
entries.new: Buy Machu Picchu entry tickets and Inca Trail permits well in advance, through official channels only.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Never hail unmarked street taxis in Lima. Use ride-hailing apps or hotel-arranged, registered taxis. Express kidnappings and robberies via informal taxis are the most common serious crime against visitors.
entries.new: Do not hail taxis on the street. The UK government warns of robberies by criminals posing as taxi drivers, especially at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport and bus terminals, and advises licensed telephone or app-based taxis, hotel-booked taxis, or the official taxi desks outside the airport baggage hall.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Tap water is not safe to drink anywhere in Peru. Stick to bottled, boiled or filtered water, including for brushing teeth in jungle areas.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller advises drinking boiled or bottled water in Peru.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Cards work in city hotels, malls and chain restaurants, but jeepneys, tricycles, markets, small eateries and most of the islands run on cash. GCash QR payments are everywhere locally but need a Philippine SIM and account.
entries.new: No official source we checked describes card acceptance in the Philippines. Canada's travel advice says ATMs are available in larger cities but may be scarce in rural areas, so have cash in pesos when you travel outside larger urban areas.
entries.note: Rewritten to Canada's advice; card acceptance set to 'limited' as no official source describes it, and the GCash claim had no source.
Canada puts May in the May–November rainy season.

entries.old: December to May is the dry season across most of the archipelago — December to February is coolest, March to May hottest. June to November brings rain and typhoons.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season runs from May to November, though storms can occur all year, and the UK government says around 20 typhoons hit the Philippines each year, mostly between June and November. No official source names a best season; the months shown fall outside the rainy season.
entries.note: May removed: Canada places it in the rainy season.

entries.old: Duty-free allowance: 2 cartons of cigarettes and 2 bottles of alcohol (up to 1 liter each) per adult. | The customs declaration is completed electronically as part of eTravel registration.
entries.new: The UK government says there are strict rules on goods taken into or out of the Philippines, and you must declare anything that may be prohibited or subject to tax or duty.
entries.note: The duty-free allowance (2 cartons of cigarettes, 2 bottles of alcohol) and the eTravel customs-declaration claim could not be confirmed.

entries.old: Book an onward or return ticket before you fly — Philippine carriers and foreign airlines alike will refuse boarding without one for visa-free travelers.
entries.new: Book an onward or return ticket before you fly: the UK government says most visitors are expected to have proof of return or onward travel and that immigration officials and airlines may ask for it.
entries.note: Softened to what the UK says: officials and airlines 'may ask', not 'will refuse boarding'.

entries.old: eTravel registration is free. Third-party sites charging a fee for the QR code are scams. Use only etravel.gov.ph.
entries.new: Register only on the official eTravel portal, etravel.gov.ph.
entries.note: The claim that fee-charging sites are scams had no source.

entries.old: Typhoon season runs roughly June to November — ferries and domestic flights get canceled at short notice, so build slack into island-hopping plans.
entries.new: The UK government says around 20 typhoons hit the Philippines each year, mostly between June and November, and Canada says authorities may suspend ferry services at short notice when a storm signal is raised, which can strand you at a port for days. Build slack into island-hopping plans.
entries.note: Attributed to the UK and Canadian advice.

entries.old: Yes. Proof of onward or return travel is a legal condition of visa-free entry, and airlines check it rigorously at check-in — passengers without it are routinely denied boarding. A cheap real ticket to any other country satisfies the rule.
entries.new: Plan on it. The UK government says most visitors are expected to have proof of return or onward travel and that immigration officials and airlines may ask for it, and Canada says customs officials may ask to see a return or onward ticket.
entries.note: The 'routinely denied boarding' and 'any cheap ticket satisfies the rule' claims had no source.

entries.old: Narcotics, pork products and pornographic material are prohibited; many medications require a prescription. Check before traveling.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says Qatar has zero tolerance for drug offences, even residual amounts, and that some medicines legal elsewhere are controlled or illegal in Qatar. To bring controlled or prescription medication, follow the Ministry of Public Health's steps, including a prescription and a medical report in English; the Ministry runs an online permit service.
entries.note: The duty-free alcohol confiscation claim and the pornography rule are not stated by an official source we could read; the others rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: E-cigarettes and vaping products are restricted — bringing them in can lead to confiscation and fines.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says it is illegal to import, sell or buy vapes and e-cigarette products, including liquids and electronic shisha pipes, whatever the quantity; customs may confiscate them, and using them can lead to arrest, a fine, prison or deportation.
entries.note: The duty-free alcohol confiscation claim and the pornography rule are not stated by an official source we could read; the others rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: From June to September temperatures routinely exceed 45°C with high humidity. Plan outdoor activities for early morning or after dark, and stay hydrated.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says high humidity and severe heat occur from June to September, and that dehydration and heatstroke can be fatal: carry enough water and plan outdoor activity for the cooler hours.
entries.note: Temperature figure is not stated by an official source; rewritten.

entries.old: Alcohol is legal only in licensed hotel bars and restaurants — never drink in public or drive after drinking (zero tolerance), and do not bring alcohol into the country, even duty-free.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says only licensed hotels, restaurants and bars can sell alcohol, the legal drinking age is 21, and drinking or being drunk in public is illegal. There is zero tolerance for drink-driving: any amount of alcohol can mean one month to 3 years in prison or a fine of QAR 10,000–50,000, and deportation.
entries.note: Duty-free import claim removed; rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Dress modestly in public places — shoulders and knees covered is the safe rule at malls, souqs and government buildings; swimwear is fine at hotel pools and beaches.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says to dress modestly in public, including while driving — men and women should cover their shoulders and knees — and that the dress code is strictly enforced in government buildings, healthcare facilities and banks, where you may be refused entry.
entries.note: Swimwear claim removed; rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Yes, but only in licensed venues — mainly hotel bars and restaurants. Drinking in public is illegal, there is zero tolerance for drink-driving, and you cannot bring alcohol into the country even from duty-free.
entries.new: Yes, but only in licensed venues: the UK FCDO says only licensed hotels, restaurants and bars can sell alcohol and the legal drinking age is 21. Drinking or being drunk in public is illegal and can bring up to 6 months in prison or a fine of up to QAR 3,000, and there is zero tolerance for drink-driving.
entries.note: Duty-free import claim removed; rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.
entries.new: Between EU countries, alcohol and tobacco bought with tax paid, for your own use and not for resale, owe no further tax, according to the EU's Your Europe portal.

Tobacco limits depend on the country, and travellers under 17 get no alcohol or tobacco allowance.

entries.old: In Bucharest use ride-hailing apps (Bolt, Uber) or order taxis through an app — overcharging of tourists at the airport and Gara de Nord is a long-running problem.

entries.old: Visa and Mastercard issued outside Russia do not work anywhere in the country. Bring US dollars or euros in cash to exchange, and budget for the whole trip. Russian-issued Mir cards are accepted almost everywhere domestically.
entries.new: The UK Foreign Office says Mastercard and Visa are not operating in Russia: cards issued outside Russia will not work in shops or ATMs, while cards issued inside Russia work only there. Paying in foreign currency is illegal; to buy roubles, take US dollars or euros and change them only at banks, hotels and exchange bureaus.
entries.note: Rewritten to the FCDO's wording; the Mir-card claim was replaced by its statement on Russian-issued cards.

entries.old: May to September brings warm weather and long daylight for Moscow, St Petersburg's White Nights and the Golden Ring towns; winter is atmospheric but very cold.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Russia. The CIA World Factbook describes a climate ranging from steppe in the south through humid continental in much of European Russia to subarctic in Siberia and tundra in the polar north.
entries.note: Withdrawn: the White Nights and Golden Ring season claims had no official source.

entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

US dollars are widely accepted at a rate close to the fixed EC$2.70.

entries.old: The official Atlantic hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30, peaking August to October. Ferries between the islands are canceled in heavy swell — build slack into island-hopping plans and check that your insurance covers weather disruption.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the hurricane season runs from early June to the end of November, and that even small tropical storms can quickly become major hurricanes. Monitor forecasts, follow local authorities, and check that your insurance covers weather disruption.
entries.note: The peak-months and ferry-cancellation claims had no source.

entries.new: Canada's travel advice says La Soufrière is an active volcano whose last significant eruption was in April 2021, and that it has limited police presence around La Soufrière and the north of the island. Monitor local media for volcanic activity and take care if trekking there.
entries.note: The claims about who publishes the alert level had no source.

entries.old: Vapes and e-cigarettes are illegal in Singapore — possession or import brings fines that can reach thousands of dollars. Leave them at home.
